close_rendering: Let the women be silent in the assemblies, for it is not permitted for them to speak; rather, let them submit, just as the law also says.
whats_happening: Paul is closing a long section on how the church in Corinth should run its meetings, where prophets and people speaking in tongues have been talking over one another. He has already told tongue-speakers and prophets to stop speaking under certain conditions, using the same verb he uses here. This verse gives the same instruction to a third group. Readers disagree about which speech, and which women, are meant.

key_words.note: Paul uses the same verb for those speaking in tongues in verse 28 and prophets in verse 30. Both times it means 'be quiet in this situation', not 'never speak'.
A general verb for speaking, used across this chapter for tongues, prophecy, and ordinary talk.
No specific text is cited, which is unusual for Paul when he appeals to the law.

translation_note: The BSB, WEB and KJV translations agree closely here. English versions differ mainly in punctuation and paragraph breaks, which change where the sentence seems to begin and end.

claims.claim: σιγάτωσαν is a present active imperative, third person plural.
The subject of σιγάτωσαν is αἱ γυναῖκες, a nominative plural.
The same verb σιγάω is used as an instruction to two other groups earlier in the chapter.

evidence.note: tongue-speakers, if no interpreter is present
a prophet, if a revelation comes to another

claims.claim: The verse sits inside a block of instructions about order in church meetings (1 Cor 14:26-40).
Earlier in the same letter Paul describes women praying and prophesying in the assembly without objecting to the practice itself.
In first-century Greek and Roman cities, women generally had less access than men to formal training in public speaking and the scriptures.
Readers disagree whether this means women in general or wives in particular.

evidence.note: the same noun covers both 'woman' and 'wife'

positions.label: Women in the assembly generally
positions.case: In verse 34, 'the women' (αἱ γυναῖκες) is not narrowed down, and the appeal to the law and to the churches is general, not about a household relationship.

positions.label: Wives specifically
positions.case: Verse 35 tells them to ask their own husbands at home. γυνή is the ordinary word for wife, so verse 35 gives the household setting the noun leaves open.

evidence.note: 'their own men' in v. 35 is the standard idiom for husbands

claims.claim: The SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) marks three places in this verse where manuscripts differ.

evidence.note: apparatus markers stand on γυναῖκες, ἐπιτρέπεται and ὑποτασσέσθωσαν

claims.claim: Manuscripts place verses 34 and 35 in two different spots, and readers disagree about where they first stood.

evidence.note: the competing placements are not supplied by the current datasets; an apparatus dataset is still to be selected

positions.label: Here, after verse 33
positions.case: Standard editions print the verses here, and most manuscripts have them here.

positions.label: After verse 40
positions.case: Some manuscripts put the two verses at the end of the chapter. Readers have used this to ask whether they were part of Paul's own argument here.

related_passages.note: The same letter pictures women praying and prophesying in the assembly.
The surrounding argument, where the same silence instruction is given to two other groups.
The other passage in the letters under Paul's name on women, teaching and quietness.
